newsitem.title: GERMANY: Top German woman politician fights sleaze charge.
newsitem.headline: Top German woman politician fights sleaze charge.

text.p: The reputation of Germany's top woman politician came under threat on Wednesday over accusations of sleaze -- just as her opinion ratings soared to make her the country's most popular politician.

For the past four days, the popular daily Bild has been running front-page stories accusing Bonn's parliamentary speaker Rita Suessmuth of misusing official aircraft to make 13 private trips in two years to see her daughter in Zurich.

Suessmuth, 59, a former university professor from the liberal wing of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), has said nine of the trips were purely for official work and pledged to account for all the flights in question.
That may not be enough in the world of Bonn intrigue, though, to keep her career as the "Mrs Clean" of German politics from crashing.

Suessmuth, second in the state hierarchy after President Roman Herzog, is not popular in the CDU. The announcement on Tuesday that the Bonn public prosecutor was considering a charge of misuse of the official planes made her even less so.
"How much longer can Kohl protect Suessmuth?" asked the conservative daily Die Welt on Wednesday, adding that names of possible successors were already circulating.

A deputy leader of the CDU group in parliament, Gerhard Friedrich, urged Suessmuth to clear up the affair quickly. "The speaker always sets high moral standards -- now she has to meet them, too," he told Bild.

"Nobody is more interested in clearing this up than myself," Suessmuth said on Tuesday evening in her first public comment on the charges. "I booked my private flights privately and financed them accordingly."
The attacks came just as Suessmuth, an earnest speaker with a preaching style, for the first time reached the top of the popularity poll published in the news magazine Der Spiegel.
Long a champion of women's rights within the CDU, she won a 10-year struggle last October when the party agreed to reserve one-third of its official posts and candidacies for women.
Many men and several younger female delegates opposed the idea, but Kohl pushed it to help raise the party's appeal among young women, the voter group where its support is weakest.
Suessmuth was a Bonn newcomer when Kohl unexpectedly named her health minister in 1985. She quickly became known through the liberal AIDS awareness campaign she launched.

When former parliamentary speaker Philipp Jenninger quit in 1988 after a controversial speech on the 50th anniversary of the Nazi's "Crystal Night" pogrom, Suessmuth was elected by a large majority to take his place.

Suessmuth, who frequently travels abroad on parliamentary business, survived a 1991 scandal about her husband's use of her official limousine. The practice was judged legal in the end but put the first dent into her "Mrs Clean" image.
